about: bridge42worlds is a site that parses scientific papers and keeps a live panel on the El Niño event of 2026-2027. Two kinds of knowledge sit behind this chat. FIRST, the panel: our own measurements and readings, rebuilt every day from public sources (NOAA OISST and CPC, ERA5, TAO/TRITON moorings, GODAS, satellite radiance, FAO food prices and more). It is organised as scenes, and each scene holds charts, indicators and short notes. On top of the raw numbers we keep four kinds of statement, and every one of them has an address you can cite: risks (a judgement with a level from 1 to 5, what it rests on and what to watch), alerts (a reading that broke a record or a threshold today), indicators of the journal (a number with its history, source and date), and units of our own statistics (a method applied to our series: trends, change points, clusters, extremes, coherence, epochs and so on). There is also a verdict of the day and a glossary. SECOND, the works: scientific papers we parsed and adapted, searched by meaning through a vector index. How to use the two. The state map below is the WHOLE structure of the panel today, not a search result: questions about what is most dangerous, what changed, what to watch, what is at a record are answered from it by sorting and picking, because similarity of words cannot rank by level or date. The vector search is for meaning: a mechanism, a term, a comparison with the literature, anything the map does not spell out. Reason from the map first, ask for a search second.

scenes.text: Briefing: the whole day in plain words, with live numbers and links.
The verdict of the day: what the panel concludes right now, and why.
Overview: every scene as a small tile with one line and a chart.
News: what changed this week, and the loud readings behind it.
Mentions: how our sources and works talk about the event.
Now: where the event stands today, with the analogue years beside it.
Ocean: sea surface by region, month by month and day by day.
Satellite: raw radiance from four instruments, deep convection over the box.
Models: the IRI plume, how the models break, and their revisions.
Air and fuel: pressure, convection, trade winds, warm water volume, the layers.
Dynamics: our daily watch series with trends, bands and change points.
Regions: what the event means for named parts of the world.
Food: FAO price indices and the lag behind the event.
Long term: the century-scale record, land and ocean, belts of the planet.

verdict: ALERT Niño 1+2 is above anything measured at +4.6 °C and Niño 3 is above anything measured at +3.5 °C. A very strong El Niño is already under way.

risks.title: A very strong El Niño is under way
risks.plain: Water in the key patch of the Pacific is 2.7 degrees warmer than normal. The threshold for a “very strong” event is two degrees.
risks.watch: the NOAA weekly index; the official ONI is now +1.80 (JJA), the “very strong” category starts at +2.0 on the three-month average.

risks.title: The fuel is at its record and has not started to burn
risks.plain: The heat that will surface later is already piled up under the equator, and it is at a record for the whole series. This is measured, not forecast: the surface has not yet shown what is already stored below.
risks.watch: the monthly PMEL update: the first clear fall of the volume is the earliest honest sign that the peak is near.

risks.title: Water +11.3 °C above normal is sitting at 100 m under 125°W
risks.plain: This is the heat that has not surfaced yet. It is measured directly, every day, and it is what makes 'the event has room to grow' a statement about the present rather than about the past events.
risks.watch: the warm anomaly moving east along the moorings and rising toward the surface; the east D20 shallowing again would mean the wave has passed.

risks.title: The event has room to grow: the fuel is charged and the analogues peaked in winter
risks.plain: Every past event of this strength peaked in winter, between mid-November and early February. It is the end of summer now, so two or three more months of growth are likely.
risks.watch: if the weekly Niño 3.4 stops rising before November, the event has reached its plateau earlier than the analogues.

risks.title: The eastern Pacific is heating, off the coast of South America
risks.plain: There are two kinds of El Niño: one heats the middle of the ocean, the other the east, off Peru and Ecuador. This is the second kind, the harshest in its consequences: 1982 and 1997 were like this.
risks.watch: the difference staying above 1 °C through September and October.

risks.title: The world ocean is warmer every day than it has ever been on that day
risks.plain: On each of the last 30 days the ocean, averaged over the planet, was warmer than on the same day of any year since 1982. Not one hot day, but an unbroken stretch.
risks.watch: the first day below the record without a change of season is the first sign of a turn.

risks.title: Niño 3.4: not a spike but a new level
risks.plain: The series did not jump and come back; it rose and stayed. The gauge that accumulates the excess over the spring level crossed its threshold 95 days ago and has only grown since.
risks.watch: if the accumulated gauge starts to fall, the regime is letting go.

risks.title: Some forecast models are already below reality
risks.plain: Of 26 models, 13 have already fallen behind what the ocean showed this week. They are not “wrong about the future”; they are not keeping up with the present.
risks.watch: the next IRI issue: how many models catch up.

risks.title: The year after the peak: 2027 is likely to be warmer than 2026
risks.plain: El Niño releases the ocean's heat into the air with a lag of a few months, so the calendar year that follows the peak is usually the warmer one. That is why 1998, 2016 and 2024 each became the warmest year measured up to that point.
risks.watch: annual land+ocean mean once the peak passes; the first months of next year already carry the signal.

risks.title: The air is answering the ocean, so the event can travel
risks.plain: El Niño is not a warm patch of water, it is a coupling: the water heats, the trade winds give way, the cloud tower moves east, and only then does the event reach harvests on the other side of the planet. All three are in place now, which is why the regional impacts on this page are worth taking seriously.
risks.watch: the same three: if the winds return and the convection moves back west, the event stays in the ocean and the teleconnections fade.

risks.title: The upper 300 m of the central and eastern Pacific hold +2.51 °C of extra heat
risks.plain: The CPC calls this the upper-ocean heat content index and watches it as the leading sign of where the surface goes next. One degree across that band is already a large charge; this is 2.5.
risks.watch: the index in the next monthly GODAS; the moorings above show it a month earlier.

risks.title: world ocean: not a spike but a new level
risks.plain: The series did not jump and come back; it rose and stayed. The gauge that accumulates the excess over the spring level crossed its threshold 62 days ago and has only grown since.
risks.watch: if the accumulated gauge starts to fall, the regime is letting go.

risks.title: land+ocean: not a spike but a new level
risks.plain: The series did not jump and come back; it rose and stayed. The gauge that accumulates the excess over the spring level crossed its threshold 35 days ago and has only grown since.
risks.watch: if the accumulated gauge starts to fall, the regime is letting go.

risks.title: world ocean: the last 30 days are the warmest in the whole record
risks.plain: For these same dates none of the 45 years was warmer. Even after subtracting the general warming, +0.33 degrees remain above it: that is what the event itself adds.
risks.watch: whether the lead holds after the change of season.

risks.title: land+ocean: the last 30 days are the warmest in the whole record
risks.plain: For these same dates none of the 87 years was warmer. Even after subtracting the general warming, +0.55 degrees remain above it: that is what the event itself adds.
risks.watch: whether the lead holds after the change of season.

risks.title: The models keep revising the forecast upward, issue after issue
risks.plain: When almost all models move their forecast in the same direction, the event is outrunning them. The shift itself is a signal: the next issue will probably be higher again.
risks.watch: the IRI issue around the 19th.

risks.title: A La Niña usually follows within a year or two
risks.plain: The ocean does not simply return to normal: after a strong El Niño it usually swings the other way. A La Niña flips the map of impacts, so the regions that are dry now tend to be wet then, and the grain exporters that had a good year tend to have a bad one.
risks.watch: the ONI trend after the peak; a fall of 0.3 or more per month is the usual signature of the swing.

risks.title: Global temperature in 2027 is likely to run above 2026; regional impacts follow their own lags
risks.plain: The dashboard measures the ocean today, but people meet an El Niño through harvests, water and prices, and those arrive with a delay of six to eighteen months. The plans that matter are for next year: import contracts, reserves, water rationing, insurance.
risks.watch: the first harvests after the peak season and the food price index six to twelve months from the onset.

risks.title: The atmosphere is still catching up: three floors follow the ocean with a 3-month delay
risks.plain: The ocean heats the air, not the other way round, and the air takes months to answer. That is why the warmest months of the whole record usually arrive AFTER the peak of an El Niño, not during it — and why the year that follows this one is the one to watch.
risks.watch: the monthly satellite layers: the tropics react first, the global mean follows.

risks.title: 2 westerly wind bursts in the last 120 days
risks.plain: Bursts are how an El Niño is fed: the warm water each one sends east surfaces off South America two to three months later. The bursts of the last four months are the ones arriving now and through the autumn.
risks.watch: a new run of five days above the threshold; the MJO entering phases 6–8 makes one more likely.

risks.title: The ocean holds more heat than ever measured (0–2000 m)
risks.plain: This is the reservoir the event draws on and returns to. A record reservoir means the statistical forecasts, trained on a cooler ocean, are reading a different system than the one they learned.
risks.watch: the next quarterly NCEI update; whether the 0–2000 m series keeps rising through the event.

alerts.title: World food prices are at a twelve-month high
alerts.detail: FAO index 133.3 in 2026-08, the highest since 2022-11; a year ago 130.0.

alerts.title: Oils prices are +16.4 % against a year ago
alerts.detail: Oils index 196.9 in 2026-08; the group most exposed to El Niño droughts in South-east Asia and southern Africa is vegetable oils.

alerts.title: Dairy prices are -21.7 % against a year ago
alerts.detail: Dairy index 119.2 in 2026-08: a fall this large moves the whole index.

alerts.title: Wheat, US HRW: +43 % against a year ago
alerts.detail: 330 $/mt in 2026-08; in the 93rd percentile of all year-on-year changes since 1960; weight 5 of 5: about a fifth of the calories people eat worldwide (FAO food balances); Kuwait imports all of its wheat.

alerts.title: Soybean oil: +32 % against a year ago
alerts.detail: 1638 $/mt in 2026-08; in the 83rd percentile of all year-on-year changes since 1960; weight 3 of 5: the second vegetable oil; also the meal behind poultry and aquaculture feed.

alerts.title: Fish meal: +19 % in a month, unusual for the season
alerts.detail: 2500 $/mt in 2026-08; the usual change for this calendar month since 1979 is -0.5 % give or take 3.7, so this is about 5 times the usual swing; +43 % against a year ago.

alerts.title: Water +11.3 °C above normal at 100 m depth, 125°W
alerts.detail: TAO mooring, five-day mean to 2026-09-01: the warm layer that will surface is already measured.

alerts.title: 14 of 26 forecast models are broken
alerts.detail: on the completed seasons of this year they came in low by 1 °C or more, or three issues in a row: CPC MRKOV, IOCAS ICM, TONGJI-ML, LDEO, XRO, CSU CLIPR….

alerts.title: The share of models below reality has grown since Aug 2025
alerts.detail: 20 % in the Aug 2025 issue → 62 % in the Jun 2026 issue, down from 71 % in the May 2026 issue; the average model error went +0.17 → -0.17 °C.

alerts.title: In the Jun 2026 issue 15 of 24 models were below reality
alerts.detail: target season JJA 2026, observed ONI +1.80; the average model was -0.17 °C off.

alerts.title: 13 models have been below reality in most issues
alerts.detail: they are not wrong about the future, they fail to keep up with the present: CPC MRKOV (10/10), MetFRANCE (9/10), IOCAS ICM (8/10), UKMO (7/10), TONGJI-ML (6/6).
